package_info.package_manager: Custom/Unknown (malware distributed via document exploits, droppers, and removable media)
package_info.package_versions: Multiple variants (see SHA1 hashes in IOCs)
package_info.why_malicious: Mongall is a backdoor malware family attributed to the Aoqin Dragon APT group, designed for cyberespionage. It is distributed via malicious documents exploiting MS Office vulnerabilities (such as CVE-2012-0158 and CVE-2010-3333), fake removable devices, and phishing lures. The malware enables persistent remote access, arbitrary command execution, and data exfiltration, and communicates with attacker-controlled C2 infrastructure using covert channels such as DNS tunneling.

execution_context.file_location: malicious Word document (exploiting CVE-2012-0158 or CVE-2010-3333)

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: Shellcode embedded in a malicious Word document exploiting CVE-2012-0158 to execute arbitrary code and drop Mongall payload.
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At document open-time, the embedded shellcode exploits a vulnerability (CVE-2012-0158 or CVE-2010-3333), executes arbitrary code to write the Mongall backdoor binary to disk, and launches the payload, resulting in initial infection and persistence.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Embedding shellcode in Office documents to exploit known vulnerabilities for arbitrary code execution is a hallmark of targeted malware campaigns and is never present in legitimate documents.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normal Word documents do not contain or execute shellcode, nor do they drop or execute external binaries.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: None; exploit code in documents is always malicious and has no legitimate use case.
key_indicators: Presence of exploit code for CVE-2012-0158 or CVE-2010-3333
Dropping and executing external binaries upon document open

execution_context.trigger: user double-clicks fake anti-virus link or opens malicious folder
execution_context.file_location: removable device or phishing lure (shortcut/link or executable)

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: Dropper executable that writes Mongall payload to disk and executes it, often using DLL hijacking or Themida packing for evasion.
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At execution-time, the dropper executable writes the Mongall backdoor binary to disk, may leverage DLL hijacking or Themida packing to evade detection, and launches the backdoor process, resulting in persistent remote access for the attacker.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Droppers that write and execute backdoor binaries, especially when launched from removable media or phishing lures, are a classic malware delivery technique and are rarely seen in legitimate software.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate software should not silently install backdoors, use DLL hijacking, or employ packing techniques like Themida for evasion, especially when executed from removable devices or phishing links.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Software updaters may drop and execute new binaries, but not from untrusted sources such as phishing lures or removable devices, nor do they use DLL hijacking for execution.
key_indicators: Writes executable to disk from removable media or phishing link
Uses DLL hijacking or Themida packing for evasion

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: Backdoor main loop: Connects to hardcoded C2 domains/IPs, receives commands, executes them (file operations, process manipulation, data exfiltration), and sends results back to C2.
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At backdoor runtime, the Mongall binary establishes outbound connections to hardcoded C2 domains or IP addresses, receives attacker commands, performs file operations, process manipulation, and data exfiltration, and transmits results back to the C2 server, enabling ongoing remote control and espionage.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Persistent C2 communication, remote command execution, and data exfiltration are core backdoor behaviors and are not found in legitimate user applications.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate software should not connect to suspicious C2 infrastructure or execute arbitrary remote commands received from the network.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Remote administration tools (RATs) may have similar features, but are not delivered via exploits or phishing and are not covertly installed.
key_indicators: Hardcoded C2 domains or IP addresses in binary

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: DNS tunneling module: Encodes C2 traffic in DNS queries/responses to evade detection.
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime during C2 communication, the Mongall backdoor encodes command-and-control traffic and exfiltrated data within custom DNS queries and responses, allowing covert communication with attacker infrastructure and bypassing standard network monitoring.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: DNS tunneling is a well-known technique for covert C2 communication and data exfiltration, rarely used by legitimate software outside of specific enterprise tunneling solutions.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normal applications do not encode command-and-control traffic or sensitive data in DNS queries or responses.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Some enterprise tools use DNS for legitimate tunneling, but not for covert C2 or data exfiltration in this context.
key_indicators: Custom DNS query/response patterns with encoded payloads
Encoded data in DNS traffic to attacker-controlled domains
Communication with suspicious or known malicious domains

attack_chain.action: Initial access via phishing document exploiting MS Office vulnerabilities or via fake removable device/dropper.
attack_chain.leads_to: Execution of Mongall backdoor on victim system

attack_chain.action: Mongall backdoor is installed and persists on the system.
Backdoor establishes C2 connection, awaits commands, and exfiltrates data.
attack_chain.leads_to: Ongoing espionage, data theft, and remote control

behavioral_signatures: Execution of shellcode or PE files from Office documents exploiting CVE-2012-0158 or CVE-2010-3333
DLL hijacking or Themida-packed binaries launched from removable media or phishing lures
Persistent outbound connections to hardcoded suspicious C2 domains or IPs
DNS tunneling activity with custom-encoded payloads in DNS queries and responses
file_indicators: Office documents exploiting CVE-2012-0158 or CVE-2010-3333
Dropper executables with SHA1 hashes listed in IOCs
Mongall backdoor binaries (multiple SHA1s in IOCs)
DLLs with suspicious loading patterns indicative of hijacking
network_indicators: Connections to C2 domains: back.satunusa.org, baomoi.vnptnet.info, bbw.fushing.org, and other domains listed in IOCs
Connections to C2 IPs: 172.111.192.233, 59.188.234.233, 64.27.4.157, and additional IPs from IOCs
Unusual DNS queries to attacker-controlled domains, with encoded data indicative of DNS tunneling
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor for Office documents exploiting known RCE vulnerabilities (CVE-2012-0158, CVE-2010-3333), execution of unknown binaries dropped from documents or removable media, and suspicious network activity including persistent connections to known C2 domains/IPs and DNS tunneling patterns with encoded payloads. Correlate file hashes with IOCs, inspect for DLL hijacking behaviors, and watch for persistence mechanisms associated with Mongall and related backdoors. Employ network traffic analysis to detect custom DNS query patterns and exfiltration attempts.
